title: My First 90 Days in IT: What I Wish Someone Had Told Me
excerpt: Onboarding is overwhelming. Here is how to turn the first three months into a launchpad instead of a blur.
body:
Your first job in IT rarely looks like the projects you built in college. There is a codebase older than you, tools you have never heard of, and acronyms in every meeting. That is normal.

1. Learn the system before you change it

Spend your first two weeks reading: architecture docs, recent pull requests, incident reports. Draw the system on paper. You will ask far better questions.

2. Keep a work journal

Write down what you did, what you learned and who helped you, every day. It becomes your appraisal material, your interview story bank, and a cure for impostor syndrome.

3. Ship something small in month one

A bug fix, a doc improvement, a test. Getting a change through review, CI and deployment teaches you the whole delivery pipeline.

4. Find two mentors

One senior engineer for technical depth, and one peer a year or two ahead of you who remembers what being new feels like.

Above all: ask questions early. Nobody expects a fresher to know everything, but everyone notices someone who stays stuck in silence.

title: Will AI Replace Entry-Level Developers? A Practical View
excerpt: AI coding assistants are changing what 'junior' work looks like. The opportunity is bigger than the threat — if you adapt.
body:
AI assistants now write boilerplate, tests and first drafts of code. That changes the entry-level job, but it does not remove it.

What is shrinking

Pure syntax work and copy-paste tasks. If your only skill is translating a spec line-by-line into code, that is at risk.

What is growing

  • Reviewing and verifying AI-generated code for correctness and security.
  • Problem framing: breaking an ambiguous business need into precise tasks.
  • Systems thinking: understanding data flow, failure modes and cost.
  • Domain knowledge in banking, healthcare, retail or manufacturing.

How to adapt

Use AI tools daily, but always be able to explain every line you commit. Strengthen fundamentals — data structures, networking, databases — because they are what lets you judge whether the AI is right.

title: Writing a Fresher Resume That Actually Gets Shortlisted
excerpt: Recruiters spend seconds on each resume. Make yours easy to scan, specific, and backed by proof.
body:
Most fresher resumes look identical: the same skills list, the same college project. Here is how to stand out.

Keep it to one page

Use a clean single-column layout so applicant tracking systems can parse it.

Lead with projects, not objectives

Replace the 'career objective' with two or three projects. For each: what you built, the tech used, and a measurable result (users, speed-up, accuracy).

Show proof

Link your GitHub, a deployed demo, or a technical blog. A live link is worth more than ten listed skills.

Tailor for every application

Mirror the keywords in the job description — honestly. If it says 'REST APIs' and you built one, say exactly that.
